title: Christ's two natures attested, then the bread taken and given
english: He is Lord in deity and in humanity, confirming the divine and human natures without confusion and without division, by divine signs and by human sufferings. When he was about to come to his voluntary, renowned, and life-giving death for us, he took bread in his holy and undefiled hands, presented it to you, God and Father, gave thanks, blessed it, sanctified it, and gave it to his disciples, to his holy ones (Matthew 26:26; Mark 14:22).

added_allusions.reason: The Greek sequence, he took bread, blessed it, and gave it to his disciples, reproduces the institution narrative frame of Matthew 26:26. Missed reference flagged by the Grok check and verified against the Greek.

The same Greek sequence, λαβὼν ἄρτον, εὐλογήσας, ἔδωκε τοῖς μαθηταῖς, reproduces Mark 14:22's wording for taking, blessing, and giving the bread. Missed reference flagged by the Grok check and verified against the Greek.

translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: The prayer continues its thanksgiving, now describing how Christ, one Lord in deity and humanity, attested both natures before his voluntary death, and then took bread and gave it to his holy disciples.

title: The Words of Institution for Bread and Cup
english: to the apostles, saying, “Take, eat; this is my body, which is being broken for you for the forgiveness of sins.” In the same way, after supper, he took the cup, having mixed it from two elements—from the fruit of the vine (Matthew 26:29; Mark 14:25) and water—sealed the cup of immortality, and gave it to his disciples, saying, “Drink from it, all of you; this is my blood of the new covenant, which is being poured out for you and for many for the forgiveness of sins (Matthew 26:26-28; Luke 22:19-20).”

added_allusions.reason: The Greek 'Take, eat; this is my body' and the cup poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins reproduce Matthew's institution wording.

Mark's account shares the common institution core, but its distinctive wording is absent and the one Markan trace, poured out for many with ὑπέρ, sits inside the conflated phrase, so the echo falls short of clear.
The Greek 'after supper' frame, the body given for you, and the cup as the new covenant reproduce Luke's institution wording.
Paul's distinctive wording, 'this cup is the new covenant in my blood' and the remembrance sayings, is absent, and every shared phrase is also Lukan, so the echo falls short of clear.
The Greek ἐκ γεννήματος ἀμπέλου, from the fruit of the vine, is the distinctive Supper phrase of Matthew 26:29. Missed reference flagged by the Grok check and verified against the Greek.
The same phrase, ἐκ τοῦ γενήματος τῆς ἀμπέλου, stands in Mark 14:25. Missed reference flagged by the Grok check and verified against the Greek.

translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: Christ, having blessed the bread, now speaks the words of institution to his apostles and then likewise blesses and gives the cup.

title: Prayer that the bread and cup become saving body and blood
english: May this bread be changed and become the body of Christ—a divine body, a body that brings salvation to souls and bodies. And may what has been mixed in this cup into one reality become the blood of Christ, the blood of the new covenant, blood that brings salvation to us. Grant this so that we may wholly share in your mysteries in newness of spirit, and not in the oldness of the letter (Romans 7:6).

added_allusions.reason: The Greek ἐν καινότητι τοῦ πνεύματος καὶ οὐχὶ παλαιότητι τοῦ γράμματος is nearly verbatim Romans 7:6.

translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
orientation: The anaphora concludes with a petition that the consecrated bread and cup may become Christ's body and blood for the salvation and participation of the faithful.
